analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour over seven years and ends separate lower minimums for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 231–199 on July 18, 2019, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $15.00 in steps over six years, and after that adjusted it each year with the growth in the typical American worker's pay so it would no longer sit frozen for decades. It would also phase out the lower minimum wages that let restaurants pay tipped workers as little as $2.13 an hour, let employers pay newly hired teenagers less, and let some employers pay workers with disabilities a subminimum wage. It passed the House in July 2019 but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage or just above it. The bill's step-by-step schedule would raise pay for regular employees to $15 an hour, and eliminate the separate lower minimums so that tipped employees, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities would eventually all be covered by the same wage floor.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $7.25 to $15.00 an hour, starting six months after enactment and reaching $15 in year six.
After reaching $15, the wage would rise each year with the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees, so it would not go another decade without an increase.
Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage, which allows restaurants to count tips toward wages as low as $2.13 an hour in cash pay, and guarantees employees the right to keep their tips.

Bars any new special certificates allowing employers to pay workers with disabilities a subminimum wage and sunsets the existing program, while directing the Labor Department to help employers and workers transition.

Requires the Labor Department to publish each wage increase 60 days before it takes effect, and directs the Government Accountability Office to report on the effects of the first increases on businesses, including small businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum or near-minimum wages — restaurants, fast food, retail, hotels, and other low-wage businesses — would face higher labor costs. Tipped-restaurant owners would lose the tip credit that lets them pay $2.13 in cash wages, and sheltered workshops would lose the ability to pay subminimum wages.

drawbacks.text: The $15 floor applies nationwide, including lower-wage states where the jump from $7.25 is largest; employers there face the steepest cost increases, and economists generally agree a wage floor set this high can lead some employers to cut jobs, hours, or automate tasks.

There is no small-business carve-out. An amendment that would have exempted enterprises with fewer than 10 employees and less than $1 million in sales failed on a 210–218 vote, so every covered employer must pay the full federal floor.

The bill sunsets subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities after a transition period, and the assistance it offers those workers is only provided 'upon request,' which leaves some workers currently in sheltered employment uncertain of where they would land.
The bill offers no offsetting tax relief or credits to small businesses to cushion the phase-in; its only compliance aid is optional technical assistance from the Labor Department.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of workers at or near the federal minimum wage, the gain is direct and large: a wage floor that rises with typical pay instead of sitting at $7.25 for a decade. The real cost falls on low-wage employers, concentrated in food service and retail, and the honest objection is the risk to jobs in the lowest-wage regions. Phasing in over six years, rather than overnight, was designed to soften that, but the bill's failure to pair the mandate with any small-business offset left its central economic risk unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on July 18, 2019, went to the Senate, was placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee approved the bill on a 28–20 vote and reported it on July 11, 2019.

On July 18, 2019, Republicans offered a motion to recommit — a last chance to amend it — that would have exempted small enterprises with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales; it failed 210–218, with 195 of 197 Republicans and 14 Democrats voting for it.
The bill passed the House that same day, 231–199, with 228 of 235 Democrats in favor and 3 of 197 Republicans joining them.

The Senate received the bill on July 18, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019. It stayed there; the Senate never debated it or voted on it for the rest of the 116th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and every bill not passed by both chambers dies at that point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal minimum wage stayed at $7.25, and the employers who would have paid more — restaurant and fast-food operators, other low-wage businesses, and holders of disability subminimum-wage certificates — kept the existing lower floor. The roughly 30 million workers the Congressional Budget Office estimated would have seen raises did not receive them.

for.name: Bobby Scott
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through his committee, which approved it 28–20 and reported it to the House floor.

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Scheduled the bill for a full House vote in July 2019, her chamber's first minimum-wage vote in a decade.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote after the House passed it.

against.name: 195 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted yes on the motion to recommit that would have exempted very small businesses, and voted no on final passage.

sides.party_line_note: On passage, 228 of 235 Democrats voted yes and 3 of 197 Republicans joined them; on the small-business amendment, 195 of 197 Republicans voted yes and 14 Democrats crossed over.

industries.note: The bill phased out the tip credit that lets restaurants pay tipped workers $2.13 an hour in cash wages, and raised the wage floor for their largely minimum-wage workforce, increasing labor costs for fast food, casual dining, and hotels that depend on tipped and low-paid staff.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and providers holding disability subminimum-wage certificates
industries.note: The bill barred new 14(c) certificates and sunset the program that allowed employers to pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage, ending a decades-old exemption these employers relied on.

industries.industry: Retail, grocery, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Businesses that pay at or near the federal minimum would see labor costs rise in annual steps to $15, with the largest increases in lower-wage states; the failed motion to recommit sought an exemption for the smallest of them.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy groups
industries.note: A higher, indexed wage floor lifts pay for the workers these groups organize and advocate for; unions supported the bill as it moved through the House.
